Element capture: any element to PNG, video or print

One call turns an ordinary element into pixels: captureElement(el), recordElement(el), exportVideo(el), printElement(el), and capturePage() for a whole ordinary page. The library puts a temporary drawable canvas in the element's place for one frame. I wanted to know what survives that, and the tests below say what does and what doesn't.

Support ticket #4821

Updated .

Type in the field, then capture. The element takes input the whole time, including while it's being recorded.

Output appears here.
import { captureElement, capturePage, recordElement, exportVideo, printElement } from '/lib/element-capture.js';

const png   = await captureElement(document.querySelector('#ticket'), { scale: 4 });
const page  = await capturePage({ full: true });          // no canvas in the page's markup
const print = await captureElement(el, { dpi: 300 });     // print-quality PNG that knows its size
const rec   = await recordElement(el, { fps: 30 });  const webm = await rec.stop();
const video = await exportVideo(el, { fps: 60 });         // WebCodecs: every animation frame, not a screen recording
await printElement(el);                                   // paginated, 200 dpi
Show the code an element to PNG, video or print
  1. An ordinary element. Nothing about it was written for canvas.
  2. One call per button. show() and img() only put the result on the page.
  3. Inside captureElement(): pick a strategy. An element already inside a drawable canvas is drawn in place. Any other element is moved into a temporary canvas for a frame.
  4. Inside: the temporary canvas. A drawable canvas takes the element's place and size, the element moves into it with moveBefore() (which keeps focus, iframes and animations), one drawElementImage() fills the canvas, and the element moves back.
  5. The whole library, with video recording, WebCodecs export and print.

A · Elements captureElement, recordElement, printElement

B · A whole ordinary page temporarily wrap body in a canvas

Each row loads a plain page (sticky header, fixed badge, content below the fold, a same-origin and a cross-origin iframe) in the frame below, scrolls it, focuses its input, and calls capturePage() with one route. A row passes when a correct image came back and scroll position, focus, caret and form value survived. Side effects are listed either way.

Twelve whole-page captures in the frame above. They scroll and focus that page, so they wait for you.

C · A folder of HTML files pickFolder, watchFolder, saveToFolder

Each .html file in a folder becomes a tile in the canvas below. Save a file in your editor and its tile redraws. "Save a PNG of every tile" writes the pictures back into the same folder. The private folder is storage that belongs to this site in your browser; it comes with three sample files and works where there is no folder picker.

No folder open.
Show the code clipboard, print margins and folders
  1. copyElement(el, { html: true }): one ClipboardItem with three types. The PNG is a promise, so the write starts inside the tap.
  2. printElement(): @page margin boxes for the header, footer and page numbers.
  3. pickFolder(), saveToFolder() and watchFolder().
  4. The tile canvas.
  5. One tile per file, redrawn when FileSystemObserver reports a change. Each file is shown in an <iframe sandbox="allow-same-origin">: its scripts don't run, and it stays same-origin so the canvas may draw it.

Findings

  • The body can be wrapped in a canvas for one frame. The snapshot is ready in the first rendering update after the canvas goes in: the paint event fires in that same frame, so the only thing to wait for is one frame.
  • The shadow-root route doesn't move any element. A shadow root on <body> holding canvas > div[drawable] > slot reprojects every body child without touching the light DOM: no mutation records for the page, selectors like body > main keep matching, focus, caret, iframes and scroll position stay put. Its cost is permanent: a shadow root can't be removed, so body keeps a bare <slot> afterwards and the page can never attach its own.
  • The move route needs moveBefore(). With it, moving body's children into a canvas and back keeps focus, caret, form state and iframes alive. With plain append the iframes reload and focus is lost, and taking an iframe out of a canvas in the frame it was drawn crashed the tab.
  • CSS animations restart when an element becomes a canvas descendant, on every route. The library reads currentTime before and seeks the restarted animations back.
  • Fixed and sticky need a stand-in viewport. A drawable element is a containing block, so fixed elements attach to it. Wrapping the content in a viewport-sized frame with an inner scroller set to the page's scroll offset gives a faithful viewport shot. In a full-page shot fixed elements land at the end of the document and sticky ones at their static position.
  • Cross-origin iframes come out blank, by design, and so do cross-origin images without CORS. Same-origin iframes paint.
  • Video doesn't have to be a screen recording. exportVideo() pauses the element's animations, steps them one frame at a time and encodes each frame with WebCodecs, so a 60 fps file has all 60 frames a second in the right place on any machine. The WebM container is written by a hundred lines of script.
  • One clipboard item can hold the picture and the content. copyElement(el, { html: true }) writes image/png, text/html and text/plain together, and navigator.clipboard.read() returns all three. The markup has to be read before the capture starts, because the capture adds temporary attributes to the element.
  • @page margin boxes work for a printed capture. Chromium 157 keeps all three boxes (@top-center, @bottom-left, @bottom-right with counter(page) and counter(pages)) on the print document.
  • A folder can be the source and the destination. FileSystemObserver reported a changed file 2 to 5 ms after the write in the test browser, once per write step. A sandboxed srcdoc iframe is drawn only with allow-same-origin; with a bare sandbox its origin is opaque and the canvas leaves it out.
  • Open: the folder picker and FileSystemObserver on Android, and HEVC recording, need a real device. The test browser records VP8, VP9, AV1 and H.264 and has no HEVC encoder.
  • Output is rasterised again at the new size. drawElementImage(el, 0, 0, w × 4, h × 4) replays the element's paint record at the new size, so a 4× PNG has sharp text and hairlines, and a printed page does too.
